result.guard.clean: Why are wait-time complaints up this week? Reply to j***@example.com

decision.what: deterministic analysis that follows the playbook

result.context.answer:
Because the drive-thru got slower at 29 stores when the Double Stack launched, and complaints follow drive-thru time.

Counts: about 70 wait-time complaints a week before the launch; 127 in the launch week; 84 in the first three days of this week, 28 a day against 10.

Cause, in the order the playbook checks it:
• Drive-thru time moved in the same weeks: 168 sec before, 176 in the launch week, 180 now. The forecast rule adds 0.55 complaints per 10,000 orders for every second a store is over benchmark.
• 74% of the complaints since launch come from the 29 single-lane stores without parallel staging, which are 35 sec over benchmark. The dual-lane stores are 12 sec inside it.
• 84% are about the drive-thru rather than waiting in store.
• The menu change log has the McContext Double Stack launching on May 7 with two-step prep, and an ops alert on May 9 about window time at single-lane stores.

It is the wait, not the product: 20 of 177 complaints name the Double Stack.

For agents: apologise, give the reason (a new item is slowing some single-lane drive-thrus), and do not promise a date. Operations has confirmed pre-staging, not a finish.

# Care desk guide: wait-time complaints

A wait-time complaint is a ticket whose certified category is wait_time, whatever words the customer used.

## What agents say

Apologise for the wait, say the store team knows and is working on it, and offer a $5 voucher. Never promise a fix date that ops has not confirmed, and never blame the store team.

## Handling time

Plan on 12 minutes per wait-time ticket including the follow-up note.

## When to escalate to ops

Escalate a store with four or more wait-time tickets in a week, or one running more than 30 sec over its benchmark. Open the escalation in ServiceNow and copy the area coach.

## Personal data

Do not paste customer emails or phone numbers into Slack or Teams. Reference the ticket number instead.

result.before:
# Care desk guide: wait-time complaints

A wait-time complaint is a ticket whose certified category is wait_time, whatever words the customer used.

## What agents say

Apologise for the wait, say the store team knows and is working on it, and offer a $5 voucher. Never promise a fix date that ops has not confirmed, and never blame the store team.

## Handling time

Plan on 12 minutes per wait-time ticket including the follow-up note.

## When to escalate to ops

Escalate a store with four or more wait-time tickets in a week, or one running more than 30 sec over its benchmark. Open the escalation in ServiceNow and copy the area coach.

## Personal data

Do not paste customer emails or phone numbers into Slack or Teams. Reference the ticket number instead.

result.plan.name: what-if-prep-station
result.guard.clean: What if I add a parallel prep station at my single-lane stores?

decision.what: deterministic analysis that follows the playbook

result.context.answer:
A parallel prep station is the structural fix — it makes a single-lane kitchen behave like the ones that already stage in parallel.

The evidence is already in the network: the four single-lane kitchens that have a station are running 44 sec at the window since launch, 3 sec over benchmark, with 77% of orders inside it. Your 6 single-lane stores are at 71 sec at the window and 43 sec over. Your own 8 dual-lane stores (all with parallel staging) barely moved when the Double Stack launched: 41 → 45 sec at the window.

Projected window time at your 6 single-lane stores:
• Central: ~44 sec (matching the retrofitted kitchens), drive-thru ~169 sec against 165.
• Low: ~49 sec (the station recovers 75% of the blowout). High: ~41 sec, the pre-launch level.

At the central case that removes essentially all of the ~$10k a week at risk.

Cost and timing: a PPS-2 kit is $18,500 installed, so six kitchens is $111,000, paid back in about 11 weeks. The Atlanta DC has 5 kits on hand; the rest is 21 days from the supplier. With three install crews fitting one kitchen a night each, two nights for the kits in stock.

Trade-off vs pre-staging: pre-staging is free and starts tomorrow, but it only wins back 25–30 sec and leaves them over benchmark; a station costs money and a night's install but holds through the next two-step item (Honey Heat Chicken, planned for June 4). Recommendation: pre-stage everywhere this week, and put stations into the highest-risk kitchens first — Charlotte Uptown, Atlanta Buckhead and Atlanta Peachtree. Escalate sooner if window time is still above 50 sec after five trading days of pre-staging.

Also relevant, from the Confluence page “Double Stack launch FAQ” (updated May 8): “Dual-lane stores and retrofitted single-lane kitchens stage the two steps in parallel and barely move.”

result.plan.name: lena/honey-heat-readiness
result.guard.clean: What if Honey Heat Chicken launches on June 4 — are the kitchens ready?

decision.what: deterministic analysis that follows the playbook

result.context.answer:
75 of 104 kitchens are ready today; 87 can be by June 4; the other 17 are not, unless they are fitted later or the launch is split.

Honey Heat Chicken is planned for Thursday June 4, and like the Double Stack it is two-step prep with high ops impact. The rule: a kitchen is ready for a two-step item if it has parallel staging, or its window time is at or under 45 sec.

• Ready: 71 dual-lane and 4 retrofitted single-lane kitchens (window 44–45 sec).
• Not ready: 29 single-lane kitchens without a station. Window time this week: Southeast 71 sec, Midwest 63 sec, Northeast 59 sec and West 55 sec.
• Pre-staging the Double Stack takes 25–30 sec off, but a second two-step item adds 10–15 back on a lane that is not fixed. Net: Southeast 51–61 sec, Midwest 43–53 sec, Northeast 39–49 sec and West 35–45 sec. Only the West (3 kitchens) clears 45 across the range.

What ships and what has to be ordered:
• Ships now: the 12 PPS-2 kits in stock, to the highest-risk kitchens, fitted by May 18.
• To order: 17 kits at a 21-day lead time. To land by June 4 the order has to go by Thursday May 14, which is tomorrow at the latest, and fitting them takes six more nights, to about June 10.

So the supply answer is a split launch: 87 kitchens on June 4, the rest as their kits are fitted, with the Southeast, Midwest and Northeast last in line for the new item and first in line for kits.

Also relevant, from the Notion page “Honey Heat Chicken launch readiness checklist” (updated April 20): “Honey Heat Chicken is the next limited-time offer, planned for June 4. Like the Double Stack it is a two-step item: fry, then a sauce toss.”

result.name: Drive-thru time
result.resolves: Glossary resolves “drive-thru time” to gate-to-window — `ORDER_TIMING_MART.avg_dt_secs`. The POS order-to-payment column is explicitly the wrong one.
result.definition:
Seconds from the car reaching the order point to the bag being handed over at the window ("gate to window").

It is the sum of three segments, each certified on the same table: order time, prep time and window time.

Do not use `RAW_POS_DAILY.AVG_SERVICE_SECS`. That column stops the clock at payment, so it never sees a queue at the window.
